opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, Peter. This is one of my favorite questions, because I think it gets at the core of what makes us different from every other animal.

Yuval Harari puts it nicely: we're the only species that can cooperate flexibly in large numbers with strangers, and the glue is fiction. Money, nations, companies, human rights: none of these exist in the physical world. You can't put a dollar under a microscope and find its value. Value exists only because millions of brains agree to hold the same story at once.

As a neuroscientist, what fascinates me is what happens in the brain when that works. In our lab we've recorded people watching the same movie or listening to the same story, and their brain activity starts to synchronize. Different people, different backgrounds, and yet their neurons fire in remarkably similar patterns at the same moments. We call it neural engagement or alignment. A good story literally makes brains more alike for a while. That's the mechanism behind shared fiction. Language isn't just transferring information. It's syncing minds.

That's an enormous power, because once brains are aligned around an idea, you can build anything on top of it. A chimpanzee can't convince another chimpanzee to give up a banana today for the promise of unlimited bananas in chimp heaven. Humans do versions of that all the time, and it lets us build cathedrals, cities, and space programs.

The flip side is that the same machinery is vulnerable. If a story can align brains toward cooperation, it can also align them toward hatred, panic, or a financial bubble. The brain doesn't have a great built-in filter for "is this story true?" It mostly asks "is this story engaging, and do the people around me believe it?" So the power comes with a responsibility, for storytellers and for each of us as listeners, to notice which fictions we're letting into our heads.

And I'd say something your audience might appreciate: Bitcoin is a perfect example. It's a story about value, encoded in math, that enough people chose to believe. Whether you love it or hate it, it shows that new shared fictions can still emerge and reshape how strangers cooperate. We haven't stopped inventing them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses brains synchronizing around stories, but does not say the brain uses the same mechanism to turn language into concepts whether imagined or real.

r002.rationale: It says money has value because millions of people agree to believe the same story.

r003.rationale: It attributes humans’ ability to cooperate in large numbers to shared fiction and says shared ideas let people build large-scale projects.

fable-5.1.text:
So, the way I think about it as a neuroscientist is this: your brain, right now, is sitting in a dark box. It has never seen light, never heard a sound. All it gets is electrical signals coming in through the wires, and from that it builds a model of the world. And the thing is, the model is already a kind of fiction. It's a story the brain tells itself about what's out there. So we are, by design, creatures that live inside narratives.

What language did is take that private fiction and make it shareable. Before language, if I had an idea in my head, it died with me, or I could maybe show you by pointing and grunting. With language, I can put something into your brain that you've never seen, never touched, and you'll act on it. I can say "there's a lion behind that hill," and you'll run, even though you never saw the lion. That's already remarkable. But the real jump, the one Harari talks about and I think he's right, is when we started saying things that don't exist at all. Not "there's a lion," but "there's a god," or "this piece of paper is worth a cow," or "we are both members of this tribe even though we've never met."

Think about money. If I take a hundred-dollar bill and look at it under a microscope, there's nothing there. It's cotton and ink. Its entire value lives inside the agreement between my brain and your brain and about eight billion other brains. And yet people will work their whole lives for it, kill for it, build cities around it. A fiction, if enough people hold it at the same time, becomes more powerful than any physical object.

And here's what I find fascinating about it from the brain side. A chimpanzee can coordinate maybe with a few dozen individuals, because coordination for them requires actual relationships, grooming, knowing each other. Humans can coordinate with millions of strangers, and the glue is shared stories. Nations, religions, corporations, Bitcoin, which I'm sure we'll get to. None of these things exist outside of the collective story. And the moment people stop believing, they vanish. The Soviet Union didn't get bombed out of existence. People just stopped telling the story.

So the power is really two things. One, you get to coordinate at a scale no other animal can touch. And two, you get to live in a world that's partly invented, which means you can change it by changing the story. That's terrifying and wonderful at the same time. It means the most important technology we ever built wasn't fire or the wheel. It was the ability to lie to each other in a way that we all agree to believe.

r001.rationale: The response says the brain builds a model of the world and language makes private ideas shareable, but does not state that the same mechanism processes imagined and real concepts.

r002.rationale: It says a bill’s value exists through an agreement shared across many people’s minds.

r003.rationale: It attributes humans’ ability to coordinate with millions of strangers to shared stories, including ideas that do not physically exist.

astra-6.text:
I think the extraordinary thing is that language allows an idea in my head to become an idea in your head. And that idea doesn’t have to correspond to something that exists in the world. I can describe something that has never existed, and suddenly we can both think about it, argue about it, and perhaps build it.

But there’s another step: we can organize our behavior around it. Think about money. The physical object isn’t what gives it its power. The power comes from our shared expectation that other people will accept it. That belief has very real consequences: people work, trade, and make plans because of it.

So “made-up” doesn’t necessarily mean false or useless. Sometimes it means something that exists because we collectively sustain it. Language lets us do that with people we’ve never met, across enormous distances and even across generations.

And the same capacity can be dangerous. We can share a story that helps millions of people cooperate, or a story that persuades them to hurt one another. The ability to spread an idea doesn’t guarantee that the idea is true, or that it’s good.

r001.rationale: The response says imagined ideas can be shared, but does not state that the brain uses the same mechanism for imagined and real concepts.

r002.rationale: It says money’s power comes from shared expectations that others will accept it and from collective belief.

r003.rationale: It links language-shared ideas to organizing behavior and coordinating people at large scale, expressing the power humans gain from organizing around made-up ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the extraordinary thing about language is that it allows us to put something in another person’s mind that isn’t physically there. I can tell you about a tree, but I can also tell you about a country, a company, or money. Those things depend on people sharing an idea and behaving as though it matters.

And “made up” doesn’t mean powerless. You can’t eat a banknote, but if we agree on what it represents, it can get you food. That shared story allows strangers to cooperate without knowing or trusting one another personally.

The same ability lets us imagine a future and then work together to create it. But it also means we can coordinate around a story that’s false or destructive. Language gives us this enormous capacity to act together; it doesn’t guarantee that what we act on is true.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes ideas that are physically present from shared ideas, but does not say the brain uses the same mechanism to represent imagined and real concepts.

r002.rationale: It says money works when people agree on what it represents.

r003.rationale: It connects language and shared stories to people coordinating and acting together, describing this as an enormous human capacity.
